wrong_belief: Variables must be declared with their data type like int x = 5
correction: Python is dynamically typed; you do not declare variable types explicitly.
Python lists are zero-indexed, meaning the first element is at index 0.

wrong_belief: Strings in Python can be modified in place (mutable)
correction: Strings in Python are immutable; modifying them creates a new string object.

wrong_belief: Assignment b = a creates an independent copy of a list
correction: Assignment b = a binds b to the same list reference in memory, not a deep copy.

wrong_belief: == and is do the exact same check
correction: == checks value equality, whereas is checks object identity in memory.

wrong_belief: Default argument values in functions are re-evaluated each call
correction: Default arguments (like def f(x=[])) are evaluated once when the function is defined, causing mutable defaults to persist.

wrong_belief: range(start, stop) includes the stop number
correction: range(start, stop) generates numbers up to stop - 1; the stop value is exclusive.

wrong_belief: Division operator / produces an integer if both operands are integers
correction: In Python 3, / always returns a float. Floor division // returns an integer.

wrong_belief: Tuples and lists are identical, just written with different brackets
correction: Tuples are immutable sequences, while lists are mutable.

wrong_belief: Dictionaries in Python are accessed using integer indices by default
correction: Dictionaries are key-value mappings accessed by keys, not ordered numeric indices.

wrong_belief: global keyword is required to read a global variable inside a function
correction: global is only needed if you want to assign or modify the global variable, not just read it.

wrong_belief: append() on a list returns the modified list
correction: append() modifies the list in place and returns None.

wrong_belief: try/except blocks catch all errors even SyntaxError at runtime
correction: SyntaxError occurs at compile/parse time before try/except executes.

wrong_belief: isinstance() and type() are completely interchangeable
correction: isinstance() checks inheritance relationships, whereas type() checks exact type.

wrong_belief: Set elements maintain insertion order like lists
correction: Sets are unordered collections of unique elements (though recent Python optimizes internals, sets are mathematically unordered).
